newsitem.title: UK: No bombs found after UK Grand National called off.
newsitem.headline: No bombs found after UK Grand National called off.

text.p: Three controlled explosions at Aintree racecourse on Saturday after IRA bomb alerts forced the cancellation of the Grand National horse race are all thought to have been on harmless packages, police said.

The Aintree race course near the northwestern English port city of Liverpool was evacuated about 30 minutes before the 3:45 p.m. (1445 GMT) start of the world-famous 4.5 mile (7.2 km) steeplechase after police received two coded bomb warnings.
Prime Minister John Major, speaking outside his Downing Street office in London, immediately condemned the Irish Republican Army guerrilla force for wrecking the race.
Liverpool's Assistant Chief Constable Paul Stephenson told a news conference the items detonated were now thought to be "innocent".
Aintree managing director Charles Barnett said the course's contingency plans had always evisaged holding the race on a Monday n if it had to be called off for any reason.
He told reporters: "We would like that to be the case but a final decision is still to be made."
Barnett is consulting with owners, trainers and other interested parties to see whether the race can go ahead.
Stephenson said that around 70,000 people had been evacuated after the calls were received and a full search was carried out. He praised Aintree officials.
Because the calls had not been specific about where devices might have been planted, cars and coaches were having to be detained overnight.
There would be a full search at first light on Sunday. But he thought it was unlikely the public could retrieve their vehicles before midday on Sunday.

Stephenson estimated that about 40,000 of the crowd were from outside the Liverpool area and believed many would have found their way home. But emergency measures were being taken to accommodate those in difficulty.

Liverpool was sstruggling to cope with an influx of stranded racegoers, many of them cold and miserable, who were forced to look for somewhere to stay until they could reclaim their cars from nearby Aintree.
Cancellation of the race sparked anger and defiance from owners, jockeys and trainers.
A tearful Jenny Pitman, trainer of such past winners as Corbieres and Royal Athlete, called for the horses to be returned to the starting gate and the race to be run.
"We cannot be held to ransom and give in to these people. We have the lunatic element here. We can't give in to them," she said.
Jockey Carl Llewellyn, due to ride Camelot King in the big race, described the situation as sick. "Whoever did this are not sportsmen," he said.
Major said the IRA's actions in forcing the race to be cancelled would set back peace efforts in Northern Ireland.
He said the guerrilla group could not now "suddenly and cynically" declare a ceasefire and expect their political representatives be admitted to peace talks on Northern Ireland in the near future.

There has been no claim of responsibility for the bomb alert that forced the cancellation of the 150th running of the Grand National and the evacuation of 60,000 racegoers, but Major said he had no doubt the IRA was to blame.
Britain has said it will not admit Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, to the Northern Ireland peace talks unless the IRA declares a lasting ceasefire.

Security sources believe the IRA, which wants an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, is trying to force Northern Ireland on to the political agenda of the British May 1 election campaign, where it has received scant attention.
Bomb warnings, also believed to be the work of the IRA, disrupted rail and underground services in London on Friday at the height of the evening rush-hour.
